paragraphs.heading: What the Deccan Traps are
paragraphs.text: The Deccan Traps are a large igneous province in west-central India and one of the largest volcanic features on Earth. Their lava erupted from multiple volcanic centres. They are built of many layers of solidified flood basalt. Together the layers are more than about 2 kilometres thick, cover about 500,000 square kilometres and have a volume of about 1 million km³.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word trap has been used in geology for rock formations like these since 1785–1795. It comes from trapp, the Swedish word for stairs, and refers to the step-like hills that form the landscape of the region. Deccan has Sanskrit origins and means "southern".

paragraphs.heading: When the lava came
paragraphs.text: The Deccan Traps started to form 66.25 million years ago, as the Cretaceous period ended. The eruptions took place over 600,000 to 800,000 years, between around 66.3 and 65.6 million years ago, across the boundary between the Cretaceous and the Paleogene. Most of the erupting happened between 66 and 65 million years ago at the Western Ghats, when lava started to pour out in fissure eruptions. Pinning down exact ages for Deccan rock is hard. One reason is that the change from one eruption event to the next may have taken only a few thousand years, and dating methods do not have enough resolution to pinpoint these events.

paragraphs.heading: Bigger in the past
paragraphs.text: The lava may once have covered far more ground. Estimates put the original area at up to 1.5 million km², about half the size of modern India. Erosion and plate tectonics reduced the region to its present size, and lava flows can now be directly observed over around 500,000 km². The Réunion hotspot is thought to be responsible, in major part, for producing the Deccan Traps. It is still active and created the modern Mascarene Islands in the Indian Ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Gases and climate
paragraphs.text: The forming of the traps released volcanic gases, particularly sulfur dioxide, and this may have contributed to climate change. An average drop in temperature of about 2 °C was recorded during this period. Because of the magnitude, some scientists, notably Gerta Keller, have speculated that these gases played a major role in the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, also called the K–Pg extinction. The theory is that sudden cooling from sulfurous volcanic gases, along with toxic gas emissions, may have contributed significantly to that mass extinction.

paragraphs.heading: Why the impact gets the blame
paragraphs.text: The current scientific consensus is that the extinction was triggered mainly by the Chicxulub impact event in North America. The impact will have raised a dust cloud that blocked sunlight, killed much of the plant life and lowered global temperature. A major criticism of the Deccan Traps as the main cause concerns timing. The extinction appears to have been geologically instantaneous worldwide, and simultaneous on land and in the sea, as would be expected from an impact; a large igneous province would be expected to give a staggered one. The view now generally accepted is that the Deccan eruptions had a minor role at most. A 2020 study even suggested that the eruptions may have partly cancelled out the climate change brought on by the impact.
